# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Phase 3: weighted tuning summary
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

# Compare weighted candidates using both their mean CV metrics and
# paired fold-level Macro-F1 differences. The paired comparison uses
# identical validation folds for every candidate.

svm_linear_weighted_results <- rbind(
  svm_linear_weighted_C_00078125$results[, svm_result_columns],
  svm_linear_weighted_C_003125$results[, svm_result_columns],
  svm_linear_weighted_C_00625$results[, svm_result_columns],
  svm_linear_weighted_C_0125$results[, svm_result_columns],
  svm_linear_weighted_C_025$results[, svm_result_columns],
  svm_linear_weighted_C_05$results[, svm_result_columns],
  svm_linear_weighted_C_2$results[, svm_result_columns],
  svm_linear_weighted_C_8$results[, svm_result_columns]
)

svm_linear_weighted_results <-
  svm_linear_weighted_results[
    order(svm_linear_weighted_results$C),
  ]

rownames(svm_linear_weighted_results) <- NULL

weighted_resample_results <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    C = 0.0078125,
    svm_linear_weighted_C_00078125$resample
  ),
  data.frame(
    C = 0.03125,
    svm_linear_weighted_C_003125$resample
  ),
  data.frame(
    C = 0.0625,
    svm_linear_weighted_C_00625$resample
  ),
  data.frame(
    C = 0.125,
    svm_linear_weighted_C_0125$resample
  ),
  data.frame(
    C = 0.25,
    svm_linear_weighted_C_025$resample
  ),
  data.frame(
    C = 0.5,
    svm_linear_weighted_C_05$resample
  ),
  data.frame(
    C = 2,
    svm_linear_weighted_C_2$resample
  ),
  data.frame(
    C = 8,
    svm_linear_weighted_C_8$resample
  )
)

stopifnot(
  !anyNA(weighted_resample_results$Macro_F1),
  all(
    table(weighted_resample_results$C) ==
      length(cv_index)
  )
)

weighted_fold_macro_f1 <- xtabs(
  Macro_F1 ~ Resample + C,
  data = weighted_resample_results
)

highest_mean_C <- svm_linear_weighted_results$C[
  which.max(svm_linear_weighted_results$Macro_F1)
]

reference_fold_results <- weighted_resample_results[
  weighted_resample_results$C == highest_mean_C,
  c("Resample", "Macro_F1")
]

names(reference_fold_results)[2] <- "Reference_Macro_F1"

paired_fold_differences <- merge(
  weighted_resample_results[
    ,
    c("C", "Resample", "Macro_F1")
  ],
  reference_fold_results,
  by = "Resample"
)

paired_fold_differences$difference_from_highest_mean <-
  paired_fold_differences$Macro_F1 -
  paired_fold_differences$Reference_Macro_F1

paired_difference_summary <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(
    split(
      paired_fold_differences,
      paired_fold_differences$C
    ),
    function(candidate_data) {
      data.frame(
        C = unique(candidate_data$C),
        mean_difference = mean(
          candidate_data$difference_from_highest_mean
        ),
        minimum_difference = min(
          candidate_data$difference_from_highest_mean
        ),
        maximum_difference = max(
          candidate_data$difference_from_highest_mean
        )
      )
    }
  )
)

rownames(paired_difference_summary) <- NULL

cat("\nWeighted Linear SVM tuning results:\n")
print(svm_linear_weighted_results)

cat("\nFold-level Macro-F1 by C:\n")
print(weighted_fold_macro_f1)

cat(
  "\nCandidate with highest mean Macro-F1:",
  highest_mean_C,
  "\n\nPaired differences relative to that candidate:\n"
)

print(
  paired_difference_summary[
    order(paired_difference_summary$C),
  ]
)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Phase 4: selected-model out-of-fold diagnostics
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

# Select the highest mean CV Macro-F1. Candidates within 0.001 of the
# maximum are treated as practically tied, and the smaller C is retained.
# All diagnostics below use predictions from held-out CV folds only.

weighted_max_macro_f1 <- max(
  svm_linear_weighted_results$Macro_F1
)

weighted_eligible_results <- svm_linear_weighted_results[
  svm_linear_weighted_results$Macro_F1 >=
    weighted_max_macro_f1 - 0.001,
]

selected_weighted_C <- min(weighted_eligible_results$C)

linear_candidate_values <- c(
  0.0078125, 0.03125, 0.0625, 0.125,
  0.25, 0.5, 2, 8
)

linear_weighted_candidate_models <- list(
  svm_linear_weighted_C_00078125,
  svm_linear_weighted_C_003125,
  svm_linear_weighted_C_00625,
  svm_linear_weighted_C_0125,
  svm_linear_weighted_C_025,
  svm_linear_weighted_C_05,
  svm_linear_weighted_C_2,
  svm_linear_weighted_C_8
)

svm_linear_selected <- linear_weighted_candidate_models[[
  match(selected_weighted_C, linear_candidate_values)
]]

stopifnot(
  setequal(
    svm_linear_unweighted_results$C,
    svm_linear_weighted_results$C
  ),
  !is.na(match(selected_weighted_C, linear_candidate_values))
)

selected_oof_predictions <- svm_linear_selected$pred[
  svm_linear_selected$pred$C == selected_weighted_C,
]

selected_class_levels <- levels(
  training_model_data$rating_tier
)

selected_oof_predictions$obs <- factor(
  selected_oof_predictions$obs,
  levels = selected_class_levels
)

selected_oof_predictions$pred <- factor(
  selected_oof_predictions$pred,
  levels = selected_class_levels
)

predictions_per_training_row <- table(
  selected_oof_predictions$rowIndex
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(selected_oof_predictions) ==
    nrow(training_model_data),
  setequal(
    selected_oof_predictions$rowIndex,
    seq_len(nrow(training_model_data))
  ),
  all(predictions_per_training_row == 1L),
  !anyNA(
    selected_oof_predictions[
      ,
      c("obs", "pred", "rowIndex", "Resample")
    ]
  )
)

svm_selected_confusion_matrix <- table(
  Observed = selected_oof_predictions$obs,
  Predicted = selected_oof_predictions$pred
)

true_positive <- diag(
  svm_selected_confusion_matrix
)

predicted_total <- colSums(
  svm_selected_confusion_matrix
)

observed_total <- rowSums(
  svm_selected_confusion_matrix
)

class_precision <- ifelse(
  predicted_total == 0,
  0,
  true_positive / predicted_total
)

class_recall <- ifelse(
  observed_total == 0,
  0,
  true_positive / observed_total
)

class_f1 <- ifelse(
  class_precision + class_recall == 0,
  0,
  2 * class_precision * class_recall /
    (class_precision + class_recall)
)

svm_selected_class_metrics <- data.frame(
  rating_tier = selected_class_levels,
  support = as.integer(observed_total),
  precision = as.numeric(class_precision),
  recall = as.numeric(class_recall),
  F1 = as.numeric(class_f1),
  row.names = NULL
)

svm_selected_pooled_metrics <- data.frame(
  metric = c(
    "Pooled_OOF_Macro_F1",
    "Pooled_OOF_Accuracy",
    "Mean_Fold_Macro_F1",
    "Mean_Fold_Accuracy"
  ),
  value = c(
    mean(class_f1),
    sum(true_positive) /
      sum(svm_selected_confusion_matrix),
    svm_linear_selected$results$Macro_F1,
    svm_linear_selected$results$Accuracy
  ),
  row.names = NULL
)

cat(
  "\nSelected weighted Linear SVM:",
  "\nC:", selected_weighted_C,
  "\nClass weights:\n"
)

cat("\nOut-of-fold class metrics:\n")
print(svm_selected_class_metrics)

cat("\nOverall out-of-fold metrics:\n")
print(svm_selected_pooled_metrics)

RBF SVM Fitting, Tuning and Improvement

RBF SVM was considered because it can represent nonlinear relationships between the predictors and rating tiers (Karatzoglou et al., 2004). The selected weighted Linear SVM value, \(C=8\), was first used as the anchor for sigma tuning.

Three sigma values were compared: {0.015625, 0.03125, 0.0625}. Sigma was selected using mean cross-validation Macro-F1; when results were within 0.001, the smaller sigma was preferred. This selected \(\sigma=0.015625\).

With sigma fixed, the targeted \(C\) grid {0.03125, 0.125, 0.5, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32} was tested. The highest mean cross-validation Macro-F1 was achieved at \(C=16\), and performance decreased at \(C=32\).

Detailed code as follows.

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Phase 7: optional RBF SVM pilot
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

# Test one weighted RBF specification to assess whether a nonlinear
# decision boundary provides enough benefit to justify further tuning.
# The preprocessing, CV folds, metric and class weights remain unchanged.

rbf_pilot_sigma <- 1 / (ncol(scaled_validation_check) - 1L)
rbf_pilot_C <- selected_weighted_C

stopifnot(
  rbf_pilot_sigma > 0,
  rbf_pilot_C > 0
)

set.seed(5018L)

svm_rbf_pilot_time <- system.time({
  svm_rbf_pilot <- train(
    scaled_recipe,
    data = training_model_data,
    method = "svmRadial",
    trControl = coarse_control_verbose,
    tuneGrid = data.frame(
      sigma = rbf_pilot_sigma,
      C = rbf_pilot_C
    ),
    metric = "Macro_F1",
    maximize = TRUE,
    class.weights = svm_class_weights
  )
})

cat(
  "\nWeighted RBF SVM pilot completed.",
  "\nC:", rbf_pilot_C,
  "\nsigma:", rbf_pilot_sigma,
  "\n\nCross-validation results:\n"
)

print(svm_rbf_pilot$results)

cat("\nElapsed time:\n")
print(svm_rbf_pilot_time)


# RBF candidate with a more localised decision boundary:
# sigma = 0.0625, while holding C and all other settings constant.

set.seed(5019L)

svm_rbf_sigma_00625_time <- system.time({
  svm_rbf_sigma_00625 <- train(
    scaled_recipe,
    data = training_model_data,
    method = "svmRadial",
    trControl = coarse_control_verbose,
    tuneGrid = data.frame(
      sigma = 0.0625,
      C = rbf_pilot_C
    ),
    metric = "Macro_F1",
    maximize = TRUE,
    class.weights = svm_class_weights
  )
})

cat(
  "\nWeighted RBF SVM candidate completed.",
  "\nC:", rbf_pilot_C,
  "\nsigma:", 0.0625,
  "\n\nCross-validation results:\n"
)

print(svm_rbf_sigma_00625$results)

cat("\nElapsed time:\n")
print(svm_rbf_sigma_00625_time)

# Final RBF sigma sensitivity candidate:
# sigma = 0.015625, with C and all other settings unchanged.

set.seed(5020L)

svm_rbf_sigma_0015625_time <- system.time({
  svm_rbf_sigma_0015625 <- train(
    scaled_recipe,
    data = training_model_data,
    method = "svmRadial",
    trControl = coarse_control_verbose,
    tuneGrid = data.frame(
      sigma = 0.015625,
      C = rbf_pilot_C
    ),
    metric = "Macro_F1",
    maximize = TRUE,
    class.weights = svm_class_weights
  )
})

cat(
  "\nWeighted RBF SVM candidate completed.",
  "\nC:", rbf_pilot_C,
  "\nsigma:", 0.015625,
  "\n\nCross-validation results:\n"
)

print(svm_rbf_sigma_0015625$results)

cat("\nElapsed time:\n")
print(svm_rbf_sigma_0015625_time)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Phase 8: RBF pilot summary and diagnostics
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

# Combine the three RBF sensitivity-analysis candidates.

selected_rbf_anchor_index <- match(

SVM Results

The comparison table and RBF tuning figure below support the SVM conclusions. Detailed tuning, timing and out-of-fold diagnostics are provided in Appendix B.

Mean provider-grouped cross-validation results for SVM candidates.
Specification Parameters Macro-F1 Accuracy Below recall Meeting recall Above recall
Unweighted Linear C = 0.0078125 0.2829 0.7372 0.0000 1.0000 0.0000
Weighted Linear C = 8 0.4398 0.7094 0.0428 0.8351 0.4793
Weighted RBF C = 16, sigma = 0.015625 0.4754 0.7049 0.1369 0.8293 0.4403

Weighted RBF SVM targeted tuning.

Compared with the weighted Linear SVM, the weighted RBF SVM increased mean cross-validation Macro-F1 from 0.4398 to 0.4754 and improved Below NQS recall from 0.0428 to 0.1369. Accuracy and Above NQS recall decreased slightly, while Below NQS remained the most difficult class to identify. All SVM results were based on provider-grouped cross-validation, and the held-out test set was not used during tuning.

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Final selected RBF out-of-fold diagnostics
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

svm_rbf_selected_predictions <- selected_rbf_model$pred
outcome_levels <- levels(training_model_data$rating_tier)

predictions_per_row <- table(
  svm_rbf_selected_predictions$rowIndex
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(svm_rbf_selected_predictions) ==
    nrow(training_model_data),
  setequal(
    svm_rbf_selected_predictions$rowIndex,
    seq_len(nrow(training_model_data))
  ),
  all(predictions_per_row == 1L),
  !anyNA(
    svm_rbf_selected_predictions[
      ,
      c("pred", "obs", "rowIndex", "Resample", "sigma", "C")
    ]
  ),
  all(svm_rbf_selected_predictions$C == selected_rbf_C),
  all(
    svm_rbf_selected_predictions$sigma ==
      selected_rbf_sigma
  )
)

svm_rbf_confusion_matrix <- table(
  Observed = factor(
    svm_rbf_selected_predictions$obs,
    levels = outcome_levels
  ),
  Predicted = factor(
    svm_rbf_selected_predictions$pred,
    levels = outcome_levels
  )
)

rbf_true_positive <- diag(svm_rbf_confusion_matrix)

rbf_precision <- ifelse(
  colSums(svm_rbf_confusion_matrix) == 0,
  0,
  rbf_true_positive /
    colSums(svm_rbf_confusion_matrix)
)

rbf_recall <- ifelse(
  rowSums(svm_rbf_confusion_matrix) == 0,
  0,
  rbf_true_positive /
    rowSums(svm_rbf_confusion_matrix)
)

rbf_class_F1 <- ifelse(
  rbf_precision + rbf_recall == 0,
  0,
  2 * rbf_precision * rbf_recall /
    (rbf_precision + rbf_recall)
)

svm_rbf_class_metrics <- data.frame(
  rating_tier = outcome_levels,
  support = as.integer(
    rowSums(svm_rbf_confusion_matrix)
  ),
  precision = as.numeric(rbf_precision),
  recall = as.numeric(rbf_recall),
  F1 = as.numeric(rbf_class_F1),
  row.names = NULL
)

svm_rbf_pooled_metrics <- data.frame(
  metric = c(
    "Pooled_OOF_Macro_F1",
    "Pooled_OOF_Accuracy",
    "Mean_Fold_Macro_F1",
    "Mean_Fold_Accuracy"
  ),
  value = c(
    mean(rbf_class_F1),
    sum(rbf_true_positive) /
      sum(svm_rbf_confusion_matrix),
    rbf_selected_result$Macro_F1,
    rbf_selected_result$Accuracy
  )
)

cat("\nFinal RBF out-of-fold confusion matrix:\n")
print(svm_rbf_confusion_matrix)

cat("\nFinal RBF out-of-fold class metrics:\n")
print(svm_rbf_class_metrics)

cat("\nFinal RBF overall metrics:\n")
print(svm_rbf_pooled_metrics)

Model Evaluation & Selection

Selection of the final model

The following table summarises the mean five-fold cross-validation performance of each candidate model on the training set:

Provider-grouped five-fold CV comparison of each candidate’s selected configuration (training set only; not held-out test results).
Model Selected configuration Mean macro-F1 Fold SD Mean accuracy Recall: Below Recall: Meeting Recall: Above
LDA Equal priors, 2 discriminants 0.4364 0.0189 0.5106 0.525 0.483 0.601
kNN k = 5, equal voting 0.4246 0.0247 0.7224 0.044 0.897 0.310
MLR (selected) Ridge, λ = 0.001, sqrt-inverse weights 0.4871 0.0180 0.7255 — — —
Random Forest mtry = 5, min node = 20, balanced weights 0.4825 0.0265 0.6302 0.290 0.674 0.605
SVM (RBF) C = 16, σ = 0.0156, sqrt-inverse weights 0.4754 0.0104 0.7049 0.137 0.829 0.440
Majority-class baseline Always predict Meeting NQS 0.2829 0.0029 0.7372 0.000 1.000 0.000

Notes: All macro-F1, SD and accuracy values come from the same five shared provider-grouped folds. kNN and Random Forest recalls are pooled out-of-fold values, whereas the others are fold means. The same folds were used for tuning and reporting, so these estimates are subject to selection optimism.

Following comparison of the candidate models, the group selected the tuned ridge MLR as its final model. On the five shared provider-grouped folds it had the highest mean CV macro-F1 (0.4871, SD 0.0180; mean accuracy 72.55%), narrowly ahead of Random Forest (0.4825) and the RBF SVM (0.4754). These gaps are smaller than the fold-to-fold variation, so the ranking is descriptive rather than a statistical win. The selection criterion was the highest mean CV macro-F1, and the MLR also provides the interpretable coefficients used in the next section. Random Forest detected more Below NQS services in CV but at much lower accuracy (63.02% against 72.55% for the MLR). The choice was made from training-set cross-validation before test scores were computed; the caveat about earlier use of the test partition is given in the next subsection.

Selected model and test evaluation

On the five shared provider-grouped folds, the corrected MLR retained the highest mean CV macro-F1 (0.4871, SD 0.0180; mean accuracy 72.55%), ahead of Random Forest (0.4825). This difference is descriptive and does not establish statistical superiority.

Before final evaluation, the original MLR functions and tuning grid were rerun with the shared split and five shared folds, because the original MLR split differed from the group’s split. The corrected ridge multinomial model used alpha = 0, lambda = 0.001 and square-root inverse-frequency class weights. Its preprocessing and class weights were learned from the training data only, and it was refitted on all 13,497 training services. Model choice and parameters were fixed before test scores were computed, and the corrected model was not tuned on the test partition. However, the project’s test partition had been exposed in earlier model work, so the results below are not a pristine independent confirmation and should be read as descriptive estimates.

test_table <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Selected ridge MLR", "Majority-class baseline"),
  `Macro-F1` = f4(c(mlr_test$macro_f1, base_test$macro_f1)),
  Accuracy = pct2(c(mlr_test$accuracy, base_test$accuracy)),
  check.names = FALSE
)

On the test partition, the selected MLR reached macro-F1 0.4542 (mean CV macro-F1 0.4871), compared with 0.2885 for the majority-class baseline. Its accuracy was lower (73.25% against 76.28%). This reflects the imbalance of the outcome: predicting Meeting NQS for every test service already gives 76.28% accuracy. Higher accuracy alone would therefore not demonstrate useful performance across all tiers.

Only 20 of 248 Below NQS services (8.1%) were detected; 209 were predicted as Meeting NQS and 19 as Above NQS. Recall was 86.5% for Meeting NQS and 39.5% for Above NQS. Consequently, this model may inform exploratory review but should not be used alone to identify below-standard services or determine regulatory action.

The folded code below is the actual split-correction, training-only tuning and fixed-model test-evaluation scripts. It is displayed rather than rerun during rendering; the tables read its saved outputs.

harmonise <- function(model, fold, f1, accuracy) {
  stopifnot(length(fold) == 5L, setequal(fold, paste0("Fold", 1:5)),
            !anyDuplicated(fold), all(is.finite(f1)), all(is.finite(accuracy)))
  data.frame(model = model, fold = fold, macro_f1 = f1, accuracy = accuracy)

Interpretation and Stakeholder Insights

Interpretation of the selected MLR

We inspected coefficients from the selected ridge MLR (shared split, \(\lambda = 0.001\)) refitted using the training partition only. In the multinomial glmnet parameterisation (Friedman et al., 2010), a coefficient for one class is not by itself an odds ratio against Meeting NQS. For a predictor \(x_j\), the log-odds contrast between two classes depends on the difference between the corresponding class coefficients, \(\beta_{j,A}-\beta_{j,B}\). The signs below therefore refer to Above versus Meeting NQS or Below versus Meeting NQS, holding other encoded predictors fixed.

For Above NQS compared with Meeting NQS, the largest coefficient differences among non-state predictors were positive for standalone preschool status (+0.362) and provider approval age (+0.320), and negative for after-school-care status (−0.618). The state indicators produced the largest negative differences (NSW −0.602, QLD −0.578, WA −0.539, VIC −0.449 and NT −0.328), meaning that services in these states had lower modelled log-odds of Above versus Meeting NQS than services in the reference state category. For Below NQS compared with Meeting NQS, recorded service approval conditions had a positive coefficient difference (+0.244), whereas provider service count had a negative difference (−0.298); Victoria showed the largest state contrast (−0.515). Approval age is a proxy based on administrative dates, not necessarily operating experience. These findings describe conditional associations learned by the fitted model, not causal effects or a ranking of determinants of quality. Numeric features and dummy-coded indicators were processed and standardised, so the coefficients should not be interpreted as effects of a one-year increase or a raw 0-to-1 switch without accounting for the relevant scaling.

Stakeholder implications and cautions

For regulators, administrative predictors may support exploratory monitoring and help identify questions for further quality-review planning. However, the selected MLR detected only 8.1% of Below NQS services on the held-out test partition (20 of 248), and its cross-validation recall for this tier was similarly low (10.2% on the original MLR split). This means that most services in this tier were not identified; it is therefore unsuitable as a stand-alone screening or compliance decision tool. For service providers, the associations can stimulate quality-improvement discussions but do not show that changing a particular administrative characteristic would raise an NQS rating. For policy researchers, this model offers a transparent benchmark for studying associations and testing whether richer information improves minority-class identification.

Any practical use would require expert oversight, assessment of subgroup performance (including across states and service types), and validation beyond this register snapshot. Predictions should supplement, not replace, formal NQS assessment.

Final Results & Conclusion

The research question asked how well administrative service and provider characteristics can classify an Australian education and care service’s recorded NQS rating tier. The answer from this analysis is: better than a majority-class guess on balanced performance, but not reliably enough for tier-level decisions. Across the five candidate models, the best mean CV macro-F1 was close to 0.4871, and the top three models (MLR, Random Forest and RBF SVM) were within about 0.01 of each other, compared with 0.2829 for the majority-class baseline. The selected ridge MLR scored a macro-F1 of 0.4542 on the 3,663-service held-out test partition, against 0.2885 for the baseline. Its test accuracy (73.25%) was lower than the baseline’s (76.28%) because the baseline predicts the dominant Meeting NQS tier every time. The test macro-F1 was lower than the mean CV macro-F1 of 0.4871, which is consistent with cross-validation estimates being somewhat optimistic after tuning and selection on the same folds, although a single test split cannot confirm this.

Performance differed sharply by tier. On the test partition the MLR identified 86.5% of Meeting NQS services and 39.5% of Above NQS services, but only 8.1% (20 of 248) of Below NQS services. Models that detected more Below NQS services in cross-validation did so at a cost in overall accuracy: Random Forest identified 29.0% of them at 63.0% accuracy, and LDA with equal priors identified 52.5% at 51.1% accuracy. The MLR coefficients suggest that approval age, standalone preschool status, after-school-care status and provider service count are associated with tier differences, but these are conditional associations in one register snapshot, not causal effects.

The model may therefore support exploratory monitoring and questions for quality-review planning, but it should not be used alone to screen services or to determine regulatory action. Several limitations apply. The outcome is highly imbalanced and treated as nominal, so the tiers’ ordering is not used. The same folds were used for tuning and reporting, which can inflate cross-validation estimates. The test partition had been exposed in earlier model work, so the test results are descriptive estimates rather than a pristine independent confirmation. Future work could add richer predictors, use ordinal or cost-sensitive methods aimed at Below NQS recall, check subgroup performance across states and service types, and validate on a later register snapshot.

  'svm_linear_tuning_results.csv', 'svm_rbf_targeted_tuning_results.csv',
  'svm_linear_best_parameters.csv', 'svm_rbf_best_parameters.csv',
  'svm_linear_resample_results.csv', 'svm_rbf_selected_resample_results.csv',
  'svm_linear_class_metrics.csv', 'svm_rbf_class_metrics.csv',
  'svm_linear_confusion_matrix.csv', 'svm_rbf_confusion_matrix.csv',
  'svm_linear_overall_metrics.csv', 'svm_rbf_overall_metrics.csv',
  'svm_linear_timing.csv', 'svm_rbf_timing.csv',
  'svm_linear_package_versions.csv'
)
for (output_file in svm_output_files) {
  saved_results <- read.csv(file.path('../outputs/models/svm', output_file),
                            check.names=FALSE)
  cat('\n\n')
  print(knitr::kable(saved_results, digits=4, caption=output_file, format='html'))
  cat('\n\n')
}
